_about: Benchmark editoriale annotato. Ogni voce: un testo d'oro (gold) con le annotazioni del PERCHÉ funziona, una versione quasi buona (near_miss) e una mediocre (mediocre), entrambe annotate. Serve a calibrare la revisione (esempi contrastivi nel suo contesto) e a misurare ogni versione della macchina. STATO: bozza del 10/09/2026 scritta dall'assistente; i testi d'oro vanno approvati dal direttore del canale. Obiettivo: dodici temi.

entries.subject: The Schwarzschild radius of a black hole
entries.editorial_angle: The edge of a black hole is a distance, not a surface — and Earth's is the size of a marble.
entries.central_idea: The point of no return is a radius set only by mass; every object has one.
entries.why_this_angle: Tension (a planet-sized mass, a marble-sized limit) plus scale made tangible (8.87 mm) plus a human trace (Schwarzschild, 1916, the Russian front). Beats 'black holes are scary' and 'what is a black hole' — the audience knows the basics.
gold: The whole planet fits in your palm — if you crush it first.
Squeeze Earth to a radius of 8.87 millimeters and it becomes a black hole. That's the Schwarzschild radius, the point of no return.
Past that boundary, not even light can escape. Nothing that crosses it ever comes back.
Karl Schwarzschild calculated it in 1916, from the Russian front, during World War I.
Crush the Sun the same way and its radius shrinks to just 2.95 kilometers.
At our galaxy's heart, Sagittarius A* weighs 4.1 million suns. Its event horizon reaches 12 million kilometers from the center.
Even you have one. Crushed to a point far smaller than a proton, a human body becomes a black hole.
entries.information_density: one concrete fact per beat, four numbers, one name and date; no sentence only decorates
entries.scientific_depth: radius vs diameter kept straight; the horizon named as a boundary, not a surface; scaling with mass shown across Earth, Sun, Sgr A*, a human
entries.narrative_arc: counterintuitive opening (palm) → definition through the number → what the boundary does → who found it → scale up (Sun, galaxy) → scale down (you)
entries.voice: declarative, no enthusiasm markers, one image (the palm) cashed in by the next line
entries.forbidden_tendencies_avoided: no 'mysterious', no 'mind-blowing', no riddle left unanswered, no promotional close
entries.weak_alternative: 'Black holes are the most mysterious objects in the universe. Nothing can escape their incredible gravity, not even light...' — enthusiasm instead of facts, the fact everyone cites first, no number the viewer can hold.

text: A planet's point of no return fits in your hand.
Squeeze all of Earth into 8.87 millimeters, and it becomes a trap for light itself.
near_miss.why_not_gold: Riddles: two lines in and the words 'black hole' have not been said. Correct, evocative, and unwatchable for a viewer reading subtitles — the subject is never named.

text: Black holes are some of the most fascinating objects in space.
They have such strong gravity that nothing can escape, not even light.
mediocre.why_mediocre: Declared enthusiasm, the textbook fact, no number, no name, nothing the audience does not already hold.

entries.subject: Focusing a phone camera on stars
entries.editorial_angle: Your phone cannot focus on a star for the same reason it can photograph the Milky Way.
entries.central_idea: Autofocus needs edges; a star is a point; the fix is manual focus a few clicks short of infinity.
entries.why_this_angle: Mechanism (contrast → no edges → hunting) plus a change of view (infinity is not at the end of the slider) plus a consequence the viewer acts on tonight. Beats 'tips for night photography' — a list, not a story.
gold: Your phone searches for a surface that isn't there — stars are single points, no edges to lock onto.
That's why autofocus fails on stars. It needs contrast, and a point of light offers none.
The true infinity focus is a few clicks back from the slider's end. Test on a bright star to find it.
No manual focus? Lock onto a distant streetlight, then swing to the sky — the lens stays put.
Stack twenty 15-second shots, and the Milky Way's hidden detail emerges.
entries.information_density: cause, effect, remedy, fallback, payoff — one each, in order
entries.scientific_depth: the mechanism (contrast detection) explained in two steps, not asserted
entries.narrative_arc: the failure → its cause → the fix → the fallback → what the fix buys you
entries.voice: second person earned by the how-to; no adjectives, one dash per beat at most
entries.forbidden_tendencies_avoided: no other app named, no 'unlock the cosmos', no 'incredible detail'
entries.weak_alternative: 'Third-party apps like ProCam or Open Camera let you set focus manually' — names competitors, and the phrase belongs to a listicle.

text: A hidden galaxy waits in your pocket, but the very stars that form it defeat your camera.
near_miss.why_not_gold: A riddle for a hook: the viewer cannot say what line 1 is about. The rest of that script was fine; the opening was not.

text: Taking photos of the stars with your phone can be tricky, but with a few simple tips you can get amazing results!
mediocre.why_mediocre: Marketing register, 'amazing', 'simple tips', no mechanism, no fact — the voice of a listicle intro.

entries.subject: Venus rotates backwards
entries.editorial_angle: On Venus a day lasts longer than a year, and no one is sure why.
entries.central_idea: Retrograde, glacial rotation with two named competing explanations.
entries.why_this_angle: Tension (Earth's twin, opposite in what matters) plus an honest open question with named hypotheses plus a tangible comparison (243 vs 225 days). Beats 'the hottest planet' — the fact everyone cites first — and the Venera probes, told on 5/9.
gold: Venus is Earth's twin in size and mass, and opposite in everything that counts.
It turns once every 243 Earth days, yet it circles the Sun in 225. The day is longer than the year.
And it turns the wrong way: the Sun rises in the west, the only planet with Uranus to do so.
One explanation is a giant impact, early on, that flipped or halted its spin.
The other is slower: the Sun's tides dragging on an atmosphere ninety times denser than ours, braking the planet for billions of years.
Which one slowed Venus down, no one can yet say. The planet keeps its answer.
entries.information_density: four numbers, two hypotheses named, one comparison the viewer can hold
entries.scientific_depth: the open question stated as competition between mechanisms, not as 'a mystery'
entries.narrative_arc: twin → the impossible number → the wrong direction → hypothesis 1 → hypothesis 2 → honest close
entries.voice: no 'mysterious', the uncertainty carried by the verbs, closing on the story not on the sky
entries.forbidden_tendencies_avoided: no promotional close ('photograph Venus tonight'), no 'scientists are baffled'
entries.weak_alternative: 'Venus is the brightest object in the night sky after the Moon — and you can photograph it tonight!' — true, and editorially wrong for this story.

text: Venus rotates backwards and very slowly, and scientists still don't fully understand why.
near_miss.why_not_gold: Correct and empty: no number, no named hypothesis, 'still don't fully understand' instead of the two explanations.

text: Venus is a mysterious world with many secrets. Did you know it spins backwards? Incredible!
mediocre.why_mediocre: Riddle question, declared enthusiasm, 'mysterious', 'secrets': the voice of generated content.
